inter_annotator_agreement.note: Direct A/B flips (5.3%) concentrated on pairs where motion quality and prompt adherence pulled in opposite directions—exactly the cases where composite reward > single-signal reward.

human_vs_automated_correlation.metric: Spearman rho (human binary preference vs automated score delta)

results.interpretation: Strongest proxy for human preference. The multi-signal reward model captures what humans care about more than any individual metric.
Good for prompt adherence but misses motion quality. Annotators frequently preferred the lower-CLIP video when it had noticeably smoother motion.
Captures motion consistency well but misses semantic mismatch between video and prompt.
Weaker predictor alone—humans don't prefer more motion, they prefer appropriate motion. High flow magnitude on static scenes is penalised by annotators.
FVD correlates moderately; limited by its population-level nature (can't rank individual pairs meaningfully).

human_vs_automated_correlation.key_finding: Reward model score (ρ=0.73) is the best single predictor of human preference, followed by CLIP (ρ=0.61). The gap between them reflects the reward model's inclusion of motion smoothness—humans penalise jitter even when the video is semantically correct.

human_automated_agreement_by_category.description: Rate at which human preference matches automated preference label, by failure mode category

categories.note: Both humans and metrics agree on jitter/flicker
